questions.stem: What is the fixative of choice for routine surgical pathology specimens, and what is the required minimum volume ratio of fixative to tissue?
options: 70% Ethanol at a 5:1 ratio
10% Neutral Buffered Formalin (NBF) at a 10:1 ratio
Normal Saline (0.9% NaCl) at a 20:1 ratio
Glutaraldehyde at a 2:1 ratio
questions.explanation: The fixative of choice for routine histology is 10% Neutral Buffered Formalin (NBF). Proper tissue preservation requires a 10:1 volume ratio of fixative to tissue. Using normal saline instead of formalin for routine histology is strictly prohibited as it leads to tissue autolysis.

questions.stem: What is the approximate tissue penetration rate of 10% Neutral Buffered Formalin, and what is the minimum required fixation duration for routine histology?
options: ~1 mm/hour penetration rate; minimum 6–8 hours fixation
~5 mm/hour penetration rate; minimum 1–2 hours fixation
~10 mm/hour penetration rate; minimum 12–15 hours fixation
~0.1 mm/hour penetration rate; minimum 48 hours fixation
questions.explanation: Formalin penetrates tissue at a rate of approximately 1 mm/hour. Standard processing requires a minimum fixation time of 6–8 hours, while 24 hours is optimal for cellular preservation and ancillary testing.

questions.stem: Why is a shave biopsy strictly contraindicated when evaluating a patient for suspected cutaneous malignant melanoma?
options: It triggers rapid hematogenous dissemination of malignant cells
It performs a horizontal cut through the superficial dermis and fails to assess deep margins
It causes immediate melanocytic cellular lysis upon air exposure
It prevents formalin fixative penetration into the dermis
questions.explanation: A shave biopsy makes a horizontal slice through the superficial dermis and does not assess deep margins. It is strictly contraindicated in suspected melanoma because determining vertical Breslow invasion depth requires an intact deep dermal margin.

questions.stem: What is the primary diagnostic limitation of Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) compared to Core Needle Biopsy (CNB)?
options: FNA carries a significantly higher risk of tissue hematoma
FNA provides no tissue architecture, making it impossible to distinguish in-situ from invasive carcinoma
FNA cannot aspirate fluid from cystic neck masses
FNA requires routine general anesthesia in an operating suite
questions.explanation: FNA collects isolated cells and fluid using a small needle, making it rapid and minimally invasive. However, because tissue architecture is not preserved, FNA cannot evaluate basement membrane integrity or differentiate in-situ carcinoma from invasive carcinoma.

questions.stem: How must a surgical tissue specimen intended for intraoperative Frozen Section (FS) consultation be handled and transported to the laboratory?
options: Submerged in 10% Neutral Buffered Formalin at room temperature
Placed in 0.9% Normal Saline for 1 hour
Sent completely fresh immediately on ice or dry (NEVER fixed in formalin)
Immersed in glutaraldehyde fixative
questions.explanation: Specimens for frozen section must NEVER be placed in formalin because chemical fixation prevents rapid intraoperative freezing and sectioning. They must be sent completely fresh immediately on ice or dry, with prior notification to the pathology lab.

questions.stem: What is the reported diagnostic sensitivity of an intraoperative frozen section biopsy, and what is its typical reporting time?
options: ~75% sensitivity; 1–2 hours reporting time
~85% sensitivity; 45–60 minutes reporting time
~95% sensitivity; 15–30 minutes reporting time
100% sensitivity; 2–5 working days reporting time
questions.explanation: Frozen section consultation provides rapid intraoperative diagnosis within 15–30 minutes with an established diagnostic sensitivity of approximately 95%.

questions.stem: According to standard surgical pathology conventions, how are short and long sutures applied to orient an excised specimen?
options: Short suture = Superior margin; Long suture = Lateral margin
Short suture = Anterior margin; Long suture = Posterior margin
Short suture = Deep margin; Long suture = Superficial margin
Short suture = Medial margin; Long suture = Inferior margin
questions.explanation: Unless an alternative convention is explicitly agreed upon with the local pathology department, the universal suture orientation standard designates a short suture at the superior margin and a long suture at the lateral margin.

questions.stem: What is the standard color-coded ink convention used by pathologists to delineate distinct surgical margins on a resected specimen?
options: Black = Anterior; Blue = Posterior; Yellow = Inferior; Green = Superior
Black = Posterior; Blue = Anterior; Yellow = Superior; Green = Inferior
Red = Superior; Green = Inferior; Blue = Lateral; Yellow = Medial
Black = Superior; Blue = Inferior; Yellow = Anterior; Green = Posterior
questions.explanation: Standard multi-color margin ink conventions use Black for posterior, Blue for anterior, Yellow for superior, and Green for inferior margins.

questions.stem: When performing an incisional biopsy of a large soft tissue mass, which area should be selected for sampling?
options: Central necrotic and hemorrhagic core
Interface of normal and abnormal viable peripheral tissue
Surrounding skin epidermis only
Overlying subcutaneous adipose layer
questions.explanation: Incisional biopsies remove a partial sample for diagnostic purposes. Key technical rules require including the junction/interface between normal and abnormal tissue while avoiding central necrotic areas, which yield non-diagnostic debris.

questions.stem: If electron microscopy analysis is specifically required for a specialized biopsy specimen, which fixative must be used?
options: Bouin's solution
Glutaraldehyde
70% Isopropanol
10% Neutral Buffered Formalin
questions.explanation: Electron microscopy requires glutaraldehyde fixation to preserve cellular ultrastructure and organelle membranes. Routine 10% NBF is unsuitable for electron microscopy studies.

questions.stem: To preserve hormone receptors (ER/PR/HER2) and immunohistochemical markers in breast resections, fixation in 10% NBF should ideally begin within what cold ischemia timeframe post-excision?
options: Within 15 minutes only
Within 1 hour post-excision (cold ischemia time ≤1 hour)
Within 6 hours post-excision
Timing does not affect receptor preservation
questions.explanation: Immunohistochemistry and hormone receptor testing yield optimal results when tissue is placed in 10% NBF within 1 hour of surgical excision (cold ischemia time ≤1 hour). Delays beyond 30–60 minutes risk protein degradation and autolysis.

questions.stem: Where should patient identification labels be physically placed on a surgical specimen container?
options: Directly on the removable lid for easy visibility
Directly on the body of the container itself (NEVER on the lid)
Tied directly around orientation sutures
Taped onto the outer biohazard transport bag only
questions.explanation: Labels must be written or placed directly on the container body, NEVER on the lid. Lids can be accidentally mismatched or swapped during processing, leading to catastrophic patient misidentification.

questions.stem: According to mandatory specimen labeling standards, how many patient identifiers are required on every surgical specimen container?
options: One identifier (Patient full name only)
At least two identifiers (e.g., Patient full name AND Date of Birth / Hospital ID)
Three identifiers including bed number and ward name
Only the surgeon's full name
questions.explanation: Best practice guidelines require at least two patient identifiers on every specimen container (e.g., patient's full name with no abbreviations, plus date of birth or hospital ID number).

questions.stem: What type of tissue artefact is caused by squeezing or grasping delicate tissue tightly with surgical forceps during excision?
options: Drying artefact
Crush artefact
Fixation artefact
Autolysis artefact
questions.explanation: Crush artefact is an artificial tissue distortion caused by mechanical squeezing with forceps. It crushes delicate cell structures and causes nuclear smearing, obscuring microscopic detail.

questions.stem: What is the primary clinical consequence of submitting a pathology request form without relevant clinical history or imaging details?
options: Immediate destruction and rejection of the tissue specimen
Non-specific reporting and failure to consider important differential diagnoses
Automatic execution of molecular DNA sequencing
Mandatory immediate repeat surgical biopsy
questions.explanation: Providing missing clinical history forces the pathologist to evaluate tissue in isolation, leading to non-specific reporting and potential failure to consider key differential diagnoses relevant to the patient's presentation.

questions.stem: Which biopsy technique yields a cylindrical full-thickness skin core (2–8 mm) encompassing epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous fat?
options: Shave biopsy
Punch biopsy
Fine needle aspiration
Core needle aspiration
questions.explanation: A punch biopsy uses a circular blade to procure a full-thickness 2–8 mm cylindrical skin sample, making it ideal for inflammatory dermatoses and pigmented lesions.

questions.stem: Why is it a strict technical rule that a surgical excision specimen must NOT be cut or sectioned (bivalved) before margin inking?
options: Cutting prevents formalin fixative from entering tissue
Inking after cutting allows ink to seep into internal cut surfaces, creating false-positive surgical margins
Cutting destroys all intracellular DNA
Inking before cutting dissolves orientation sutures
questions.explanation: Specimens must be oriented and inked BEFORE any sectioning or bivalving occurs. Cutting tissue prior to inking allows dark ink to flow into internal surgical cuts, which the pathologist will misinterpret under the microscope as a positive resection margin.

questions.stem: What is the standard routine turnaround time (TAT) for small diagnostic biopsies versus large, complex surgical resection specimens?
options: Small biopsies: 15–30 minutes; Large specimens: 1–3 working days
Small biopsies: 1–3 working days; Large or complex specimens: 5–10 working days or longer
Small biopsies: 5–10 working days; Large specimens: 24 hours
Both take 3–4 weeks
questions.explanation: Routine turnaround time for small biopsies is 1–3 working days. Large or complex specimens require 5–10 working days or longer due to extensive grossing, fixation time, and potential special/immunohistochemical stains.

questions.stem: Which of the following diagnostic procedures CANNOT be performed on a formalin-fixed (10% NBF) specimen?
options: Routine H&E histological evaluation
Flow cytometry for suspected lymphoma and microbiology bacterial culture
Diagnostic immunohistochemical cytokeratin staining
Pathological TNM staging
questions.explanation: Flow cytometry (which requires live intact cells) and microbiology cultures (which require viable microbes) CANNOT be performed on formalin-fixed tissue. Formalin cross-links proteins and kills microorganisms; these procedures require fresh, unfixed tissue.

questions.stem: According to the golden rules of specimen orientation, when should orientation sutures ideally be placed by the surgeon?
options: After the specimen has been fixed in formalin for 24 hours
While the specimen is still in situ prior to complete surgical detachment
In the pathology laboratory after gross sectioning
Only if a positive margin is identified on permanent section
questions.explanation: Golden Rule #3 dictates that orientation should be established while the specimen is still in situ prior to complete excision. Once a soft-tissue mass is detached, it collapses and rotates, making retrospective orientation prone to error.
